items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: The only time I ever worked with him was with the Les Hite Band... I came down and joined them.

ctx.x: Did you ever work with him again after that?

No, not really, as a part of his band. The only time I ever worked with him was with the Les Hite Band out at the old Sebastian's Cotton Club, because after that, he had his own groups and he went his way and I went another way. The closest I ever got to him was, I worked under

the same manager, Joe Glazer, (PHONETIC) worked with Lionel Hampton as Louis Armstrong did, because he was under Joe Glazer also. So, we would cross paths quite often and we turned out to be excellent friends and we always had a mutual admiration society between he and I because he was such a fine guy and very comical and always had something going. Just a great man.

items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: Then, when he died, Les Height became the house band for Sebastian's Cotton Club... he went into the Height band and got there just before I went there.

ctx.x: The guy that played the alto on that was Les Height.

Oh. In the book, Count Basie and His Orchestra by ________, it says that during the 1930s, the Height band was frequently called upon to accompany Louie Armstrong on the recordings which the solo trumpet star was contracted to make for the Okay (PHONETIC) label and Marshal Royal was one of the musicians who contributed the background supports for such acknowledged Armstrong classics as "Confessin'" and "I'm a Ding-Dong Daddy." items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: When you worked in his band at the Apex

ctx.x: Oh, he was one of the slickest business-

men ever known outside of the Jewish locality. We used to call him a black Jew. He knew how to maneuver and knew business. If he had -- if only he had been a white man, he would have been a multimillionaire because he knew how to maneuver things.
When you worked in his band at the Apex, did he actually play or was (inaudible)? he just, . . . ?
